entry.title: Re-deriving a bundle
entry.content:
tik rederive checks a bundle and recomputes what its facts imply — at a terminal, or over HTTP with a badge that names the derivation.

verify.sh answers one question: are these bytes what they claim to be? tik rederive answers the other one: what do they add up to?

tik rederive evidence.tgz

bundle sha256-04a0bf413895fefb1c20e9231632fbc0d0a0d768275b42c097581ed19365973a
  format    tik-evidence-bundle version 1
  ticket    e26a1d57-6643-4564-99fa-8968ced7afa5  "2026.8.6132954"
  events    10
  judged by release sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca

verification
  ok   … hashes to its name and is schema-valid
  ok   every referenced parent is present
  ok   exactly one root event
  ok   … verifies as ci
  ok   ci is bound to its key by repo:metio/tik:ref:refs/heads/main, per …
  => the bytes are what they claim to be

derivation at 2026-08-06T20:29:26.198Z
  reached   :attested, :built, :scanned
  current   :attested, :scanned
  :built
      ✓ [:fact [:version]]
      ✓ [:signed-by :ci [:commit]]
      ✓ [:artifact "checksums/"]
  :scanned
      ✓ [:attested-within :vulnerability-scan "P1D"]

It takes a .tgz, an unpacked directory, or an https URL, and exits 1 when the bundle fails to verify — a derivation over bytes that are not what they claim to be is worth nothing. --edn prints the same result as data.

A bundle whose roles.edn is present but does not read as a role register is refused with exit 1 and nothing derived from it; the service answers such a bundle with status 400. Without roles.edn, the definition’s members stand (see Bundle format ).

Derivation names its instant

reached above is what the pinned rules grant at the instant printed under it. The release process demands a vulnerability scan attested within a day; a month from now the same archive, byte for byte, derives :built alone — the scan it carries is real, signed, and too old for the rule that reads it.

That is the reason to re-derive rather than record. A stored “passed” survives its own evidence; a derivation ages with it.

Gating on a bundle

Three flags turn re-derivation into a check a consumer’s own CI can stand on:

tik rederive https://example.com/evidence.tgz \
  --expect-stage :published \
  --expect-definition sha256-3c577f361a46ec2166b7f4d6fb875d2de4e317f478d425eb4ae39f77fdcb9aca

Exit 0 when every named stage is reached under that exact definition, 1 otherwise, with a line saying which expectation failed and what was derived instead.

Pin the definition. A bundle carries the rules that judged it, so a supplier who writes those rules can reach any stage they choose — :published becomes a claim about a process only once the reader names which process. That is why --expect-definition takes the full hash and refuses an abbreviation: eight hex characters is thirty-two bits for somebody to collide with deliberately, and the value is pasted into a workflow file once.

Name who may bind a key. A key the bundle earned through an identity binding was accepted under the supplier’s binding policy and checked against issuer keys the supplier shipped, and the supplier chose both. A token signed by a key the supplier made up can name any issuer and subject. --expect-bindings applies your policy and your keys instead. The policy has the shape oidc.edn uses:

{:bindings {"ci" [{:issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
                   :subject "repo:supplier/proj:ref:refs/heads/main"}]}}

tik rederive evidence.tgz --expect-bindings reader-oidc.edn

The issuer keys are read from jwks/ beside that file, the layout a tik store root already has, so a reader who runs tik points at their own oidc.edn and pins issuers with tik bridge jwks. Every bound key must then come from an issuer and subject your file permits for that actor, with a token a key you pinned for that issuer signed. A subject ending in * admits every subject that starts with what precedes it. A bundle whose signers are all listed in its actors file passes and says that no signer rests on a binding. A file without :bindings, or one that does not parse, is refused: a policy that says nothing would pass every bundle.

In GitHub Actions

permissions:
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/install@2026.8.7062815
  - uses: metio/tik/.github/actions/verify@2026.8.7062815
    with:
      bundle: https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz
      expect-stage: ":published"
      expect-definition: "sha256-3c577f36…"

The ref you pin is the tik you get: with no version input, the installer resolves the release matching its own ref, so a pinned action and a pinned tool are one decision rather than two.

The installer verifies before it trusts. It fetches the release’s SHA256SUMS, checks the cosign keyless signature naming the release workflow that produced it, and only then checks the binary against those checksums — an installer for a verification tool has no business asking you to trust an unverified download. Linux/amd64 gets the native binary; other platforms get the portable jar and need a JDK already on PATH.

verify needs tik on PATH and does one thing with it, so bring your own build if you have one.

The service

tik rederive --serve --port 7788

POST /rederive                     the bundle as the request body -> EDN
GET  /derivation?bundle=<url>      fetch it, re-derive, render the page
GET  /badge.svg?bundle=<url>       the same, as a badge

Every request re-derives. The one thing held between requests is a cache keyed by the bundle’s content address and the minute the answer was computed for — both inputs to the derivation, both immutable, so an entry is either exactly right or absent and the whole cache is disposable.

The service fetches https URLs whose every resolved address is public, follows at most four redirects, checking each hop, and caps what it will download. It runs nothing from inside a bundle: the verify.sh that travels in an archive is a convenience for whoever chooses to run it, and the service implements the checks itself.

Point a README badge at a release artifact:

[![evidence](https://your-host/badge.svg?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)](https://your-host/derivation?bundle=https://github.com/you/proj/releases/download/v1/evidence.tgz)

What a badge says

The stages the pinned definition grants, and which definition granted them: release@3c577f36 · :attested · :scanned. The badge links to a page carrying the guards that held, the ones that did not, who may sign in this bundle and on whose say-so, and the two commands that reach the same answer with the service switched off.

A badge is a derived conclusion displayed as though it were a fact, which is the one thing derived beats declared forbids storing. Three properties keep it honest:

  • it is derived per request, so it is a lens rather than a status;
  • it names the derivation — stages, definition hash, instant — where a word like compliant would name a policy it cannot see;
  • the service is disposable. Delete it and the bundle still checks out with coreutils. A verification service that becomes the authority has re-introduced exactly the trust the bundle removes.

The colour follows the same rule: one shade for a bundle that verifies, red for one that does not. Green would read as approval, and the badge reports a derivation, which is a different kind of claim.

Publishing bundles from CI

The wedge is one line over evidence a pipeline already produces. tik’s own release workflow records the version, the commit, the image digest and the checksums file as signed facts, imports the SBOM, provenance and scan as attestations through tik bridge intoto, and ships the result:

tik bundle "$TICKET" --out "evidence-$VERSION.tgz"

CI signs with an ephemeral key bound to its workload identity (ADR 0023 ), so the bundle carries the binding and its issuer’s key, and a recipient re-earns that trust from the issuer’s own signature.

entry.title: Reading a store
entry.content:
The inbox, the board, explain, selectors, history, and counterfactuals.

Every view here is computed when you ask, so none of them can be stale.

What should I do?

tik next --actor alice
tik next --role :triager
tik explain 3184 --actor alice

next ranks by how much downstream work each step unlocks, with quiet tickets rising. A step that would replace a fact already settled, such as offering :declined on a request whose decision is :accepted, is marked (overrides a settled fact), names the value it replaces on each ticket, and ranks after every step that only adds evidence:

set [:outcome :evidence]  (claude, seb)    unlocks 5
    7087c27e -> :delivered  (see: kb/runbooks/request-delivered.md)
set [:handling :reason]  (claude, seb)     unlocks 6  (overrides a settled fact)
    7087c27e -> :declined  replacing [:handling :decision] = :accepted

explain is the per-ticket answer: what is missing, whose signature it needs, and which stages it blocks. See Explain for the model behind them.

The board

tik ls
tik ls --all --long
tik ls --where 'stage=:blocked and fact:severity=:high and not disputed'
tik search firefox login

A selector is space-separated terms, all ANDed, each optionally negated: stage=:blocked, fact:severity, fact:severity=:high, actor=seb, disputed, conflicted, unsigned, derived-from=<hash>, ~text. The same grammar drives search, and tik dupes reports near-title lookalikes.

One ticket

tik status 3184
tik status 3184 --at 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z
tik log 3184
tik diff 3184 5

status reports the derived stage, the facts behind it, links, and what is next. --at answers the same question about any past moment by evaluating that moment. diff shows the evidence gained over the last few events.

Why, and what if

tik causal 3184
tik whatif 3184 severity=:low +P2D retract:category
tik debug 3184

causal names the signed events that made each reached stage true — including negations and time saying so honestly. whatif shows the stage diff a change would produce and writes nothing. debug shows the fixpoint with its working: every sweep, every guard verdict.

The roadmap and the wider picture

tik plan
tik plan roadmap.html
tik roles
tik work week --actor alice

plan derives the dependency-link roadmap — ready, blocked, done, cyclic, the critical path, and each item’s unlock impact. roles shows who gates what: every role on the open board, its effective members, and the stages waiting on its signature.

Sharing what you see

tik board board.html
tik serve --port 8080
tik bundle 3184 --out ticket-3184.tgz
tik rederive ticket-3184.tgz

board renders the whole store into one dependency-free HTML file you can mail or archive. serve publishes it live, read-only, with /tickets.edn and /explain/<id>.edn for tools. bundle packs one ticket — events, signatures, witness marks, the pinned ruleset, and a verify.sh — into a tarball a third party checks with coreutils and ssh-keygen, no tik required. rederive is the other half: it checks a bundle and recomputes what its facts imply under the rules the ticket pinned, at the instant you ask. See Evidence .

entry.title: Recording work
entry.content:
Creating tickets, asserting facts, attaching evidence, and correcting the record.

You record evidence. Stages follow.

Create a ticket

tik new support-request --title "login fails on Firefox"

The ticket pins the process definition’s content hash at creation, so it is judged by the rules it was minted under until somebody deliberately moves it with tik reprocess.

Created beneath a store, a ticket inherits its context as signed facts: repo=<name> from the enclosing git repository, plus any .tik-facts.edn maps on the way down, nearest winning, with anything explicit beating both.

Assert facts

tik set 3184 severity=:high resolution.ref=abc123def456

Dotted keys nest, so parked.reason="waiting on legal" writes the path [:parked :reason]. Values parse as EDN, and a bare word becomes a keyword — severity=high and severity=:high mean the same thing, which keeps facts out of the swamp of free-form strings.

Links are facts too:

tik set 3184 link.depends-on=9c21f0a4

tik next then holds 3184 back while 9c21 is unsettled, and tik status names the blocker.

Attach evidence

tik attach 3184 ./crash-repro.sh
tik comment 3184 reproduced on a clean profile, video attached

Artifacts are stored by hash. A comment is an artifact too — a text blob attached by its digest — which is why comments need no event type of their own.

Correct the record

Nothing is edited or deleted. Corrections are new events:

tik set 3184 severity=:critical              # supersedes; history retained
tik retract 3184 resolution.ref --reason "wrong commit"
tik dispute 3184 category --reason "this is billing"
tik dispute 3184 category --withdraw         # take back your own objection

A later assertion supersedes an earlier one. A retraction says the claim should not exist and offers no replacement. A dispute rejects the value its author saw when they raised it, so only a different value answers it. In every case the stage regresses by derivation — there is no rollback step.

Signed claims and attestations

tik attest 3184 {:ci :green}

An attestation is a signed claim whose meaning the kernel does not interpret. Lenses read it, and the :attested-within guard checks that a fresh-enough one exists — a replayed “CI green” from last month is cryptographically valid and fails that guard honestly.

Review in one batch

tik review review.verdict=approved --list
tik review review.verdict=approved

A reviewer’s queue is mostly signatures over work somebody else already recorded: a merge commit an agent asserted, a definition nobody has published yet. tik review lists everything that waits on you alone and signs it after one confirmation, or without asking when you pass --yes.

A ticket is offered when every reason its next stage gives is either your signature on a fact already on record or a fact you pass as k=v. Approving re-asserts each recorded value exactly as it stands, so the signature names the commit or hash it covers, and the list shows every value before you confirm. A dry run must show the stage landing and no reached stage lost, otherwise the ticket is left for a manual tik set. A fact the ticket’s process does not declare is ignored, so one verdict can serve several processes at once.

Arguments without = narrow the batch to a process name or a ticket id prefix. Publishing a definition needs a key, given with --key or TIK_KEY.

Each fact is one signature, so with a security key a list of forty tickets is forty touches. --batch signs the tickets with one:

tik review review.verdict=approved --batch

Your key signs a single delegation on the identity registry. It names a throwaway key, the exact ticket heads in the list, and the fact paths the list sets, and it is valid for five minutes. The throwaway key is made in a private temporary directory, signs every fact, and is deleted afterwards. A ticket that changed after the list was drawn makes the batch sign nothing, because the delegation would cover an event you did not see. With several identity-registry tickets in the store, pass --registry <id>. Definitions are still signed one by one with your key. tik verify credits the facts to you as described under Store administration .

Derive facts from the world

tik probe 3184

A probe is any executable that prints key=value lines. It runs with its working directory in the ticket’s [:repo] repository, and changed values land as ordinary signed facts, so a ticket regresses on its own when reality does. The environment carries TIK_TICKET, TIK_REPO, and every present fact as TIK_FACT_<PATH>, which is what lets one repository hold many subjects — a package, tenant, or workload per ticket. A probe has ten minutes and 1 MiB of output: past the deadline it and every process it started are killed and the probe counts as failed, and longer output is refused rather than cut. Scope scripts and population commands get the same ten minutes.

Recurring and bulk work

tik recur weekly-review --period 2026-W32
tik rollout dependency-audit --parent-title "Q3 audit"

recur mints this period’s ticket exactly once: it creates only when no ticket already carries that period label. The schedule lives outside the log — run it from cron or a timer — and tik derives whether the period exists yet. rollout creates one ticket per git repository under the store, wired to a parent by link facts, so the parent is a checklist whose checkmarks derive from each child’s evidence. Re-runs create tickets only for repositories without one, so scheduling rollout keeps the checklist current as repositories appear. A scheduled run takes --period (the labels recur reads) or --at: the ticket ids and every claimed instant then follow from the process, the repository, the actor, and the period, and two replicas running the same rollout write identical events.

Standing rules

A rule that every repository of a kind must satisfy, such as “every Go module has a README”, is a process run per repository. The process’s :scope selects the population and its :probe observes the evidence:

{:process/id :readme-present
 :scope "probes/go-module.sh"     ; test -f go.mod
 :probe "probes/readme.sh"        ; prints readme=:present or readme=:absent
 :process/facts {[:readme] [:enum :present :absent]}
 :process/stages
 [{:stage/id :tracked :guards []}
  {:stage/id :holds :after [:tracked]
   :guards [[:fact= [:readme] :present]]}
  {:stage/id :retired :after [:tracked] :stage/sticky? true
   :guards [[:fact [:population :left]]]}]
 ...}

rollout asks the scope once per repository, with the working directory in that repository and TIK_REPO set: exit 0 includes it, exit 1 leaves it out, and any other exit is reported and leaves that repository out of the run with exit code 1. --scope replaces the definition’s scope for one run. Scheduling rollout --period … and probe keeps the rule current: a repository that joins the population gets its own ticket and starts short of :holds, and a compliant repository falls back from :holds when its probe observes the README gone, since :holds is not sticky. tik status <parent> counts the children per stage, and --links holds lists the compliant ones.

A repository that is deleted, or that the scope now answers 1 for, has left the population. rollout lists such tickets on every run, and with --retire it records a signed [:population :left] fact naming the reason, repository absent or outside the scope. The :retired stage above turns that fact into a sticky terminal stage, which settles the ticket: the inbox and probe sweeps leave it alone, and its history stays in the log. A repository that comes back gets a fresh ticket, and the parent’s link points at it. An unanswered scope check never retires anything. Retiring is a separate flag because a checkout that lacks some repositories looks exactly like a store whose repositories were deleted, so a scheduled run passes --retire only where the checkout is complete.

Populations without git

A rollout’s members do not have to be git repositories. Declare a population in populations.edn in the store root, beside actors, and name it with --population, or with :population in the definition:

{:products {:list ["klimpi" "cloud-portal" "Sales training"
                   {:subject "aro" :dir "aro"}]}
 :repos    {:command "aro list | cut -f1,4"}
 :staging  {:command "netbox-hosts --cluster staging"}}

A :list names its members directly, as strings or as maps of :subject and an optional :dir. A :command runs in the directory that holds the store and prints one member per line, as subject or subject<TAB>dir. A command that fails stops the rollout before anything is written, so --retire never acts on a population nobody could read.

The definition’s :subject names the fact each child carries, such as :host or [:project]; it defaults to [:project] for a population and [:repo] for the git walk. A member whose directory lies below the store’s holder also gets [:repo], so its probe runs there. A member without a directory is probed from the holder, with TIK_SUBJECT naming it. A member whose directory is missing or outside the holder is reported and left out of the run, and rollout exits 1.

{:process/id :host-patch
 :subject :host
 :population :staging
 :probe "probes/kernel-version.sh"   ; reads $TIK_SUBJECT
 ...}

tik rollout host-patch --period 2026-W47 then mints one ticket per host of the staging cluster. A member that drops out of the population is reported as no longer in population staging, and --retire records it.

entry.title: Store administration
entry.content:
Identity, roles, verification, migration, storage backends, and alerts.

Identity

tik actor add alice ~/.config/tik/id_ed25519.pub
tik sign 3184
tik witness 3184

actor add registers a signer in the store’s allowed-signers registry. An actor name is letters, digits and ._@+-, and the key file holds one OpenSSH public key on one line; anything else is refused, because the name and key are written verbatim into the registry, where *, ?, ! and , are principal patterns and a line break starts another grant. A rung-2 binding (tik bridge oidc, tik bridge workload) whose actor or key fails the same check grants nothing.

The registry may also be edited by hand, with OpenSSH’s allowed-signers options. tik reads Ed25519 signatures in process and honours them as ssh-keygen does: namespaces="…" is a pattern list where * and ? are wildcards and a matching !pattern refuses, a cert-authority line never accepts a direct signature by the CA key, and a line with an option OpenSSH does not know grants nothing. A line carrying valid-before or valid-after depends on the time of the check, so verify hands it to ssh-keygen, and reports the signature unchecked on a host without one.

A hardware security key works as a signer too. Generate a key that lives on the device, register its public half, and point TIK_KEY at the key handle; every signature then needs a touch, and with -O verify-required the device PIN as well:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O verify-required -f ~/.config/tik/id_ed25519_sk
tik actor add alice ~/.config/tik/id_ed25519_sk.pub

tik verifies these signatures in process and counts one only when the device reports that a user was present, a flag inside the signed bytes. ssh-keygen -Y verify accepts a security-key signature made without a touch, so verify and the bundle’s verify.sh read the flag themselves. That holds for an ECDSA security key (ecdsa-sk) too: tik reads its flag in process, and only a touched signature is passed on to ssh-keygen for the cryptographic check.

Exporting TIK_KEY signs every write as it happens; sign catches up on your own earlier events, and only your own — signing somebody else’s would assert something false. witness countersigns a ticket’s head, and one signature timestamps the entire ancestry beneath it.

Roles

tik roles
tik roles add triager alice
tik roles remove triager bob

A process definition declares which roles exist and who starts in them; the store’s register decides who is in one today, for every ticket at once. Use it for a hire or a departure — it takes effect on in-flight tickets immediately, with no definition version bump and no per-ticket migration. See Roles and authority .

Verification

tik verify
tik verify --changed
tik root --witness

verify runs the ladder: content addressing, schema, signatures, and re-derivation. --changed skips unchanged heads for a fast drift check rather than the full audit. root prints one hash committing to the entire store, optionally countersigned, optionally anchored to a third-party timestamp.

A review verdict can also be signed by a throwaway key the reviewer delegated to for one batch (ADR 0037). The delegation is an attestation on the identity registry:

{:claim :delegation
 :delegation/public-key "ssh-ed25519 AAAA…"
 :delegation/not-after #inst "2026-11-23T20:04:00Z"
 :delegation/scope #{[#uuid "…" "sha256-…"]}
 :delegation/facts #{[:review :verdict]}}

verify credits a signature by that key to the reviewer only when the delegation is signed with a key actors grants the reviewer, and the verdict lies inside it. The verdict must name the reviewer as its actor, be claimed no more than five minutes after the delegation, and sit on a ticket and head pair the scope lists. It must also assert a fact path the delegation allows. A key granted through an identity binding or another delegation cannot delegate. With {:delegation {:require-touch true}} in oidc.edn, the delegation must come from a touched security key. The :delegation map holds exactly :require-touch with true or false; any other key, a missing one or another value makes the setting malformed, and a malformed setting credits no delegation at all. A delegation that credits nothing is named in the output with the reason.

An event can also carry a post-quantum signature, an ML-DSA-65 sidecar <id>.pqsig.<fpr> beside its SSHSIG one. verify checks every such sidecar against pq-signers in the store root, which holds one line per key:

seb namespaces="tik-*" ml-dsa-65 MIIHsjALBglghkgBZQMEAxID…

The key is the base64 DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, and <fpr> is the hex SHA-256 of that DER. namespaces takes comma-separated patterns where * is the only wildcard and every other character, brackets included, stands for itself. A sidecar that does not verify, names a key pq-signers lacks, or a key registered for another actor fails the audit, and so does a malformed line. A store without the file is checked as before.

To sign with ML-DSA-65, make a key with OpenSSL 3.5 or later, register its public half, and point TIK_PQ_KEY at the private key:

openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-65 -out ~/.config/tik/id_ml_dsa_65.pem
echo "seb namespaces=\"tik-*\" ml-dsa-65 $(openssl pkey -in ~/.config/tik/id_ml_dsa_65.pem -pubout -outform DER | base64 -w0)" >> pq-signers
export TIK_PQ_KEY=~/.config/tik/id_ml_dsa_65.pem

Every write then carries both signatures. A write whose TIK_PQ_KEY pq-signers does not grant the actor is refused before anything is stored. tik sign <id> with TIK_PQ_KEY adds the sidecar to your own events that lack one, which is how events written earlier gain it.

Requiring post-quantum signatures

signatures.edn in the store root makes the second signature a requirement from a chosen instant on:

{:require #{:ssh-ed25519 :ml-dsa-65} :from #inst "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"}

:from is written with seconds, at most three fraction digits, and Z or a UTC offset in hours and minutes, such as #inst "2026-12-01T00:00:00+01:00". verify, rederive and the bundle’s verify.sh read only that spelling, so they always name the same instant; lower case, a leap second, 24:00 and an instant before 1970 make the file malformed.

An event claimed at or after :from must carry a verifying signature by its own actor for every algorithm in :require. An event claimed before it needs the classical signature only, and must be anchored: it or a later event in its ticket carries an ML-DSA-65 witness countersignature, which seals the whole ancestry. Once Ed25519 can be forged, anyone can write a new event with an old instant; the anchor tells that event apart from the history that existed when the policy took effect. :require always keeps :ssh-ed25519, so the scheme stays hybrid, and a file that does not read as exactly this shape fails verify rather than counting as no policy.

Switch it on in this order, with a key pq-signers allows to witness (the tik-* pattern covers both tik-event and tik-witness):

echo '{:require #{:ssh-ed25519 :ml-dsa-65} :from #inst "2026-12-01T00:00:00Z"}' > signatures.edn
TIK_PQ_KEY=~/.config/tik/id_ml_dsa_65.pem tik anchor
tik verify

tik anchor writes <head>.pqwitness.<fpr> on every head of every ticket. Anchor again whenever events claimed before :from were written after the last anchor; verify names each event no anchor covers. Under the policy, a write without TIK_KEY or, from :from on, without TIK_PQ_KEY is refused before anything is stored. tik review --batch meets the policy when TIK_PQ_KEY is set: its verdicts carry the throwaway key’s delegated Ed25519 signature and an ML-DSA-65 signature by the reviewer’s own key.

Moving tickets to newer rules

tik reprocess 3184 processes/support-request.edn
tik reprocess 3184 processes/support-request.edn --apply

A ticket is judged by the rules it was minted under, so a definition that grows leaves existing tickets deriving under the old one until you move them — deliberately, because an implicit upgrade would re-judge a whole store on an edit. The dry run prints the pinned-versus-proposed hashes, which stages would be gained or would regress, and the new blockers. --apply records the re-pin as a signed event, so the log keeps which rules judged the ticket when.

Storage

tik init --sqlite
tik store migrate --to file
tik export ./audit-copy
tik pack
tik gc --apply

The file store is the signed interchange format; SQLite keeps the same events in one file. Migration is lossless in both directions — events, their detached signatures and the attached blobs travel together. A file store keeps a ticket’s blobs in tickets/<id>/blobs/; a SQLite store keeps them in blobs/<id>/ beside tik.db. export materializes any store as the file format. pack consolidates settled tickets into one content-addressed pack each, and gc removes archived definitions no ticket pins any more and no named definition is at, together with their publication signatures.

Handing a ticket to someone else

tik bundle 3184 --out evidence.tgz
tik import evidence.tgz
tik rederive evidence.tgz

bundle packs one ticket as an evidence bundle : the events, their signatures, the pinned definition and the registry, checkable with coreutils. import brings someone else’s events into this store, merging by content address so importing twice is a no-op. rederive recomputes what a bundle’s facts imply without importing anything.

Alerts out, mail in

tik effects run --config effects.edn --dry-run
tik bridge email < message.eml

effects run pushes derived stage transitions to Slack, Discord, Matrix, Teams, ntfy, PagerDuty, plain webhooks, email, or any program through the command sink. Any sink field may be a secret resolved at send time — from an environment variable, a file, a command, or a systemd credential — so no secret sits in the config file.

The email bridge turns messages into tickets and comments, and replies carrying tik> key=value lines become facts, which closes the loop for people who never leave their inbox.

The gated agent surface

tik agent actions 3184 --actor bot
tik agent set 3184 severity=:high --actor bot
